summary.text: Evaluating the recurrence through \(n=20\) shows that \(13^2=169\) divides \(a(20)\). Since 13 is coprime to both 2 and 3, any factorization \(a(20)=2^r3^s m\) would force \(13^2\mid m\), contradicting the squarefreeness of \(m\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\ell(x)\) denote the number of decimal digits of the nonnegative integer \(x\), with the convention \(\ell(0)=1\). Concatenating \(x\) followed by \(y\) therefore gives
\[
 C(x,y)=x10^{\ell(y)}+y.
\]
The sequence begins with \(a_1=0\), \(a_2=1\), and for \(n\geq 3\),
\[
 a_n=\left|C(a_{n-1},a_{n-2})-C(a_{n-2},a_{n-1})\right|.
\]
Equivalently, if
\[
 E_n=a_{n-1}\bigl(10^{\ell(a_{n-2})}-1\bigr)
      -a_{n-2}\bigl(10^{\ell(a_{n-1})}-1\bigr),
\]
then \(a_n=|E_n|\).

We will show that \(13^2=169\) divides \(a_{20}\). This makes the asserted squarefree-factor representation impossible, because neither a power of \(2\) nor a power of \(3\) contains a factor \(13\).

Here is the finite recurrence computation through index \(20\). In the table,
\[
 L_n=\ell(a_n),\qquad r_n\equiv a_n\pmod {169},\qquad
 q_n\equiv 10^{L_n}\pmod {169}.
\]
The last column gives the sign of \(E_n\), before taking the absolute value.

\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r|c}
 n&L_n&r_n&q_n&\operatorname{sign}(E_n)\\ \hline
 1&1&0&10&--\\
 2&1&1&10&--\\
 3&1&9&10&+\\
 4&2&72&100&+\\
 5&3&74&155&-\\
 6&5&44&121&-\\
 7&8&93&165&+\\
 8&13&112&23&-\\
 9&19&98&114&+\\
10&32&147&87&+\\
11&51&98&116&-\\
12&83&27&121&-\\
13&133&133&153&+\\
14&216&26&92&+\\
15&349&39&49&-\\
16&565&65&114&-\\
17&913&104&153&-\\
18&1478&13&35&+\\
19&2391&39&116&-\\
20&3869&0&4&-
\end{array}
\]

For completeness, this table is obtained directly from the displayed recurrence as follows. Once \(a_{n-2}\) and \(a_{n-1}\) have been computed, form the integer \(E_n\), determine its sign, and set \(a_n=|E_n|\). The decimal inequalities
\[
10^{L_n-1}\leq a_n<10^{L_n}
\]
(for nonzero \(a_n\)) determine the recorded length \(L_n\). For the modular part of the same computation, if \(\varepsilon_n=1\) when \(E_n>0\) and \(\varepsilon_n=-1\) when \(E_n<0\), then
\[
 r_n\equiv \varepsilon_n
 \left(r_{n-1}(q_{n-2}-1)-r_{n-2}(q_{n-1}-1)\right)
 \pmod {169}.
\]
Thus only the lengths, signs, and residues in preceding rows are needed to check each modular entry. The values \(q_n\) are ordinary modular powers \(10^{L_n}\bmod 169\).

The initial exact values, which also illustrate the simultaneous calculation of lengths and signs, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
1&0\\
2&1\\
3&9\\
4&72\\
5&243\\
6&47871\\
7&23523372\\
8&2434786275501\\
9&8244905115337247871\\
10&58101188398354233807319449027630\\
11&243478627550182449084906698122045988902204111779759\\
12&33753325643335988898828779215425644588407139004473126805509723691755094884662752129.
\end{array}
\]
For example,
\[
E_3=1(10^1-1)-0(10^1-1)=9,
\]
so \(a_3=9\). Next,
\[
E_4=9(10^1-1)-1(10^1-1)=72,
\]
whereas
\[
E_5=72(10^1-1)-9(10^2-1)=648-891=-243,
\]
so the absolute value gives \(a_5=243\). These examples explain in particular why the sign column is needed when propagating residues.

As another check on a later row, the row for \(n=13\) follows modulo \(169\) from the rows for \(11\) and \(12\): because \(E_{13}>0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{13}
&\equiv r_{12}(q_{11}-1)-r_{11}(q_{12}-1)\\
&\equiv 27(116-1)-98(121-1)\\
&=3105-11760\\
&\equiv 133\pmod {169}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All the other intermediate residue rows are obtained by the same displayed formula.

Most importantly, consider the final step. The preceding rows give
\[
 r_{18}=13,\quad q_{18}=35,\qquad
 r_{19}=39,\quad q_{19}=116,
\]
and the exact recurrence comparison gives \(E_{20}<0\). Before applying the absolute value, its residue is
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{20}
&\equiv r_{19}(q_{18}-1)-r_{18}(q_{19}-1)\pmod {169}\\
&\equiv 39(35-1)-13(116-1)\\
&=39\cdot34-13\cdot115\\
&=1326-1495\\
&=-169\equiv0\pmod {169}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Changing the sign by taking an absolute value does not change a zero residue. Hence
\[
 a_{20}\equiv0\pmod {169},
\]
or equivalently,
\[
13^2\mid a_{20}.
\]

Now suppose, as the conjecture requires at every index greater than \(2\), that there were nonnegative integers \(r,s\) and a squarefree nonnegative integer \(m\) such that
\[
 a_{20}=2^r3^s m.
\]
Since \(13\) is distinct from both \(2\) and \(3\),
\[
\gcd(13^2,2^r3^s)=1.
\]
We have already proved that \(13^2\mid a_{20}=2^r3^s m\). Euclid's coprime-divisor principle therefore implies
\[
13^2\mid m.
\]
Indeed, a divisor coprime to one factor of a product must divide the other factor.

But \(13\) is not a unit and \(13^2\) is the square of the nonunit \(13\). A squarefree integer cannot be divisible by the square of a nonunit (equivalently, it cannot be divisible by the square of any prime). Thus \(13^2\mid m\) contradicts the assumption that \(m\) is squarefree.

Consequently \(a_{20}\) has no representation \(2^r3^s m\) with \(m\) squarefree. Since \(20>2\), this single term contradicts the claimed universal statement. The additional divisibility-by-\(3\) clause cannot rescue the conjunction: its squarefree-factor clause already fails at \(n=20\). Therefore the conjecture is false.
